# What Could Cause a Single-Cylinder Misfire Sometimes at Idle, Always Under Load on a 2007 Toyota Yaris?

You've already performed the standard isolation tests: new spark plugs resolved the initial multi-cylinder issue, coil swaps ruled out the ignition module, and resistance checks confirm all injectors are within spec (13.2 Â± 0.1 Ohms). The misfire has narrowed down to Cylinder 3 (P0303), appearing intermittently at idle but reliably triggering under high loadâspecifically during hard acceleration on ramps or left-hand turns on inclines.

The freeze frame data is telling: STFT1 is at -5.5%, LTFT1 is elevated at 12.5%, and engine load hits 86.3% when the code sets. The fact that the misfire only occurs under specific load conditions points toward a component that struggles to keep up with demand rather than a static vacuum leak or a dead coil.

### Evaluating the Fuel Injector Under Load

Your suspicion about the fuel injector is technically sound given the symptoms. While the "click-click-click" test often fails to distinguish between a weak injector and a healthy one, it doesn't account for flow rate variance under pressure. A failing injector might still actuate (making noise) but deliver an inconsistent pulse width when the ECU demands high volume.

To validate this without immediately replacing the part, perform a balance-of-flow test. Disconnect the fuel rail and attach a low-pressure hose to each injector. Have someone crank the engine while you observe the spray pattern and listen for the distinct "chug" of the pump working against a restriction. If Cylinder 3 produces a weaker spray or requires more cranking time to start, that confirms flow deficiency.

Alternatively, use an oscilloscope to monitor the injector drive signal versus the actual injector current waveform (if your scanner supports live data logging). Look for "sawtooth" patterns that differ significantly between Cylinder 3 and a known good cylinder. This is more definitive than swapping injectors blindly.

### Investigating Vacuum Leaks and Intake Issues

Elevated Long Term Fuel Trim (LTFT1: 12.5%) indicates the ECU is constantly enriching the mixture to compensate for unmetered air entering the engine. If this trim is fluctuating wildly or only appears under load, consider that the intake manifold gasket on Cylinder 3 might be failing specifically when the manifold expands due to heat and pressure.

Check for vacuum leaks near the throttle body and the EGR valve. On older Toyota engines, cracked rubber boots or leaking PCV hoses can cause lean conditions that manifest as misfires only when the engine is under stress. Ensure the intake manifold gasket isn't failing at the cylinder head interface. A simple smoke test with a handheld smoke machine (or even soapy water on suspected gaskets) can reveal escaping air that isn't visible during visual inspection.

### Addressing the Left-Turn Misfire Pattern

The correlation between left-hand turns and inclines is a critical diagnostic clue. When you turn left, the fuel rail experiences additional G-force to the right (away from Cylinder 3's location on many inline-four layouts). If the injector or its mounting bracket has a loose connection, this lateral force could momentarily break the electrical ground or disrupt the flow path.

Inspect the injector harness connector for corrosion or loose pins. Also, check if the fuel rail clamps are tight; vibration combined with lateral G-force can cause micro-movements that affect fuel delivery timing. Ensure that the wiring from the ECU to Cylinder 3 isn't rubbing against a sharp edge inside the engine bay, as chafed wires often fail under tension or specific vibration frequencies.

### Data Interpretation and Next Steps

The upstream O2 sensor temperature readings are within expected ranges for this application; the proximity to the heat shield explains the higher readings compared to vehicles with more distance between sensors. The catalytic converter isn't clogged (pressure < 2psi), so backpressure isn't the culprit.

Before swapping injectors, which involves removing intake components and risking new leaks, verify the electrical connection at the injector itself. Disconnect the connector on Cylinder 3 and inspect for carbon buildup or moisture inside the mating port. Clean it thoroughly with contact cleaner. If the misfire persists after cleaning connections and verifying no vacuum leaks, then proceed with swapping the fuel injector from a known good cylinder (like Cyl 1) into Cyl 3. Monitor the live data stream; if the STFT on Cylinder 3 normalizes or drops significantly, you've found the root cause.

If the problem remains elusive after these checks, consider that the ECU's power supply to the injector driver might be weak, though this is rare. However, given the consistent pattern under load and G-force, a flow-restricted injector or a marginal electrical connection in the harness are the most probable culprits.
